title: Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet with IFENN: A Generalized Framework for Coupled Poroelasticity Problems
authors: Fouad M. Amin, Rigoberto Moncada, Panos Pantidis, Diab W. Abueidda, Fan Fei, Mostafa E. Mobasher
abstract: Complex, high-dimensional, large-scale poroelasticity simulations using traditional numerical solvers can be prohibitively expensive in terms of computational resources. We introduce an innovative framework for poroelasticity problems that integrates physics-informed machine learning (PI-ML) models with high-performance FEM solvers. This integration is achieved through the Integrated Finite Element Neural Network (IFENN) setup, which uses a staggered scheme between an FEM solver for mechanical equilibrium and a PI-ML model for fluid-flow predictions. We introduce a novel Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet (PIF-MIONet) architecture, in which a fusion network encodes the outputs of the MIONet branches. The MIONet encodes different input functions, and the fusion network enables early interaction between the inputs, supporting generalization across multiple scenarios while adhering to the underlying physics of the poroelasticity problem. We study different examples, covering 2D and 3D domains and considering variable material properties and time discretizations. We test the models on unseen loading histories, demonstrating accuracy and generalizability across scenarios. For complex geometries and boundary conditions, we show that with both physics and data considered in the loss function, a PI-ML model can be trained using only 0.1\% of the training increments used for pure data-driven training. In addition, we expand the PIF-MIONet to incorporate a domain decomposition approach, which was found to be particularly useful when modeling flow over more complex geometries with more localized phenomena. For the first time, IFENN is implemented using the open-source multiphysics simulator GEOS for the FEM part, providing a path for the framework's application to industrial-scale simulations and complex multiphysics problems.

infographic.key_insight: PIF-MIONet combines interacting input-function encoders with physics-informed learning to predict fluid flow within an FEM-coupled poroelasticity framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets costly coupled poroelasticity simulations while retaining FEM for mechanical equilibrium and enabling integration with the open-source GEOS simulator.
method: Stagger FEM mechanical-equilibrium solves with neural fluid-flow predictions through IFENN.
Fuse MIONet branch outputs to enable early interaction among input functions.
Combine physics and data losses, with domain decomposition for complex geometries and localized flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests cover 2D and 3D domains, variable material properties and time discretizations, and unseen loading histories; for complex cases, physics-plus-data training used only 0.1% of the training increments used in purely data-driven training.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify end-to-end speedup or establish industrial-scale performance; the reported training-increment reduction is not a runtime reduction.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Fusion-MIONet with IFENN: A Generalized Framework for Coupled Poroelasticity Problems

title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
authors: Hongrui Chen, Kittipong Thiamchaiboonthawee, Zhen Wei, Amin Heyrani Nobari, Faez Ahmed
abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.

infographic.key_insight: OAT3D generates high-resolution 3D structural topologies using a generative model designed to accommodate varying domain shapes, resolutions, loads, and supports.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It accelerates candidate generation for structural topology optimization, with a reported 3.65× speedup over conventional optimization when targeting similar compliance.
method: Sparse encoding represents load and support conditions.
A sparse volumetric variational autoencoder learns compact topology representations.
A conditional diffusion transformer generates structural designs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training uses 501,865 optimized topologies produced with 51,800 GPU-hours; the abstract reports generation at 512³ resolution and 44.9× faster raw candidate generation.
infographic.watch_item: Raw generation speed does not imply equivalent structural performance; generated designs still require engineering validation.
infographic.paper_title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization

title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
authors: Xiang Meng, Shuhei Shinzato, Zhiqiang Zhao, Linfeng Yu, Jian Guo, Liangli Chu
abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $γ/α_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $α_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.

infographic.key_insight: Boron redistributes toward defects and disordered regions in TiAl, where it pins dislocations and suppresses deformation twinning to strengthen the alloy at high temperature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling boron content and defect structure could improve TiAl’s high-temperature strength, while brittle borides and termination-dependent interface adhesion require attention.
method: Develop a high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential.
Use hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics to study boron redistribution.
Analyze deformation, defect interactions, and stacking-fault energetics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Polycrystalline TiAl simulations show a 9.4% increase in average flow stress at 1 at.% boron and 900 K, accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation.
infographic.watch_item: The reported strengthening is simulation-based; experimental validation and transferability across processing conditions remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys

title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
authors: Sikha O K, Abdollah Moslemi, Elham Alizadeh, Ludovic Humbert, Miguel A. Gonzalez Ballester, Jerome Noailly
abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid GCN-SAGE-Residual model predicts element-wise femoral stress while capturing finite element mesh topology.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate offers a computationally efficient route to FEM-based orthopedic assessment and fracture-risk analysis.
method: Represent femoral finite element meshes as graph-structured data.
Combine graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning.
Predict stress at the mesh-element level.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a primary comparison of 14 models, supplemented by architectural ablation, the hybrid achieved the best reported performance: R² = 0.8022 and MAE = 2.879 MPa.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify dataset size or external validation, leaving generalization to unseen anatomies and loading conditions uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis

title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction
authors: Yuan Zhang, Mohammad Amin Nabian, Shaotong Fu, Yiding Liu, Chengcheng Chu, Xuelin Tao
abstract: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.

infographic.key_insight: Topology-guided regional latent dynamics enable full-field transient response prediction while preserving structural organization and learning history-dependent behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: TPLD supports surrogate prediction of nonlinear structural responses, including crash deformation, on finite element meshes with up to approximately 1.49 million nodes.
method: Encode nodal responses into coupled regional latent states using mesh topology and engineering priors.
Use auxiliary one-step prediction to improve latent dynamical predictability.
Predict load-conditioned trajectories with spatiotemporal Mamba and reconstruct nodal fields with a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on three FEM datasets, TPLD reports displacement-component relative L2 errors of 4.00–8.21% for a stiffened panel and 1.41–12.22% for a vehicle model; BIW position error is 0.620%, a 30.7% reduction versus the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration.
infographic.watch_item: Regional representations depend on mesh topology and engineering priors; transfer to unseen geometries or loading regimes is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
authors: Konstantinos Dovelos
abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

infographic.key_insight: A small independent checker converts admissible potential and exactly charge-conserving current fields into guaranteed error bounds for PDE outputs from conventional solvers, LLM-written code, and neural surrogates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-based certificates can expose incorrect simulation results that pass grid-convergence studies, helping engineers audit automated computational pipelines.
method: Require each solver to provide a potential–current certificate.
Check admissibility and exact charge conservation against a written physics specification.
Compute guaranteed per-output error bounds, including for reduced-basis neural predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The checker rejected or refuted all five convergent buggy solvers; reduced-basis neural predictions received bounds at most 0.0021% wide in-range and 0.3–25% wide out-of-range, where 90% conformal intervals covered none of 14 tests.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees apply only to the stated model; informative bounds require energy-accurate outputs on a resolving grid, and free-nodal neural outputs produced valid but uninformative bounds.
infographic.paper_title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates

title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows
authors: Harald Garcke, Yifei Li, Robert Nürnberg, Quan Zhao
abstract: We introduce a geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation for the $L^2$-gradient flow of a class of curvature-dependent energies of closed hypersurfaces, where the energy density depends on the mean curvature and the unit normal. A square-root auxiliary variable converts the geometric energy into a quadratic functional. Combining its evolution equation with a skew-symmetric treatment of surface transport yields a weak formulation whose energy law depends only on the normal velocity and is therefore independent of the chosen tangential motion. We construct monolithic nonlinear parametric finite element methods by coupling a common IEQ discretization with one of two geometric formulations that accommodate either the Barrett-Garcke-Nürnberg (BGN) tangential velocity or the minimal-deformation-rate (MDR) tangential velocity. Both fully discrete approximations satisfy an unconditional decay estimate for the discrete quadratic energy. We further extend the construction to anisotropic Willmore flow, and to $H^{-1}$-gradient flows. A variety of numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of the introduced methods.

infographic.key_insight: A geometric invariant energy quadratization (IEQ) formulation enables curvature-driven surface-flow schemes with unconditional discrete energy decay, independent of the chosen tangential motion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports energy-stable finite element simulation of evolving interfaces governed by curvature- and orientation-dependent energies.
method: Introduce a square-root auxiliary variable to express the geometric energy as a quadratic functional.
Combine auxiliary-variable evolution with skew-symmetric surface transport.
Construct monolithic nonlinear parametric FEM schemes with BGN or minimal-deformation-rate tangential velocities.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments demonstrating robustness and accuracy, alongside unconditional discrete energy-decay estimates for both schemes.
infographic.watch_item: Unconditional energy decay does not establish time-step-independent accuracy; the schemes also require monolithic nonlinear solves.
infographic.paper_title: A geometric-IEQ approach for curvature-driven flows

title: Sparse Constitutive Neural Networks for Hyperelasticity
authors: Hendrik Geisler, Clément Jailin, Emmanuel Baranger
abstract: Constitutive model identification aims to recover compact, interpretable models that accurately describe material behavior. In this work, we identify hyperelastic constitutive models using artificial neural networks with sparsity-promoting constraints and regularization. The proposed method combines the expressiveness of neural networks with the structural interpretability of sparse constitutive models, such as those identified by EUCLID, by representing the strain energy density as a sum of products of univariate functions of the invariants. The resulting decomposition exposes the contributions of individual invariants and their interactions. The method is demonstrated on synthetic data in supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios, showing that it can accurately identify interpretable constitutive models with few active modes.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse neural networks identify compact hyperelastic strain-energy models while exposing individual invariant contributions and their interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports interpretable constitutive model identification for describing nonlinear elastic material behavior.
method: Represent strain-energy density as a sum of products of univariate invariant functions.
Apply sparsity-promoting constraints and regularization to retain few active modes.
Identify models in supervised and unsupervised learning settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic-data demonstrations in both learning settings show accurate, interpretable model identification with few active modes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports only synthetic-data validation, so robustness to experimental noise and real-material complexity remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Constitutive Neural Networks for Hyperelasticity

title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning
authors: Antonio Varagnolo, Miaomiao Dai, Bolei Deng, Raphaël Pestourie
abstract: Designing mechanical metamaterials for nonlinear behavior such as energy absorption is limited by high-dimensional parametrizations and by expensive simulations. Here we show that design knowledge from a cheap linear property can be transferred to nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable, targets through a learned, reusable search space. TRAMA (TRAnsferable representation learning for Metamaterial Architectures) reparametrizes architected materials using a variational autoencoder with a pre-trained vision transformer and physics-informed augmentations. For energy-absorption efficiency, TRAMA reaches every efficiency level with 95 to 98% reduction in the evaluations needed by state-of-the-art gradient-free optimization and 3 to 5 fewer than gradient-based optimization. Its best design is comparable to the best found by any baseline with at least 67% fewer evaluations, which translate into approximately 100 hours saved per campaign with finite-element simulations. Fabricated designs match simulated stress-strain curves within 5.3%. A post hoc analysis shows where the representation transfers to new properties and where it does not.

infographic.key_insight: TRAMA transfers knowledge from a cheap linear property into a reusable learned design space for optimizing nonlinear mechanical metamaterial behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces costly simulation evaluations for energy-absorbing metamaterial design, saving approximately 100 hours per finite-element optimization campaign.
method: Learn a compact architecture representation using a variational autoencoder and a pre-trained vision transformer.
Use physics-informed augmentations to support representation learning.
Transfer the learned search space to nonlinear, potentially non-differentiable design objectives.

infographic.watch_item: Transferability is property-dependent; the learned representation does not support all new targets equally well.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Optimization of Mechanical Metamaterials via Transferable Representation Learning

title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
authors: Alexandra Starostina, Alexander Hermann, Mahish Guru, Kartik Bali, Roland Aydin, Christian C. Cyron
abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM-guided redesign of a magnesium stent reduced a high-percentile bend-strain objective by 32% while navigating about 1,650 CAD parameters within 15 simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach suggests a route to coordinated component redesign when nonlinear simulations are expensive and manual parameter reduction may constrain optimization.
method: GPT-6 Astra proposed coordinated edits to the stent’s CAD parameters.
Each proposal was built, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact.
Full simulation results informed subsequent design proposals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Within the same 15-simulation budget, Tosca improved the objective by about 10%; a separate higher-fidelity deployment check of an earlier LLM design found 14% lower strain and 63% less damage at its most damaged spot.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to one component study, and the higher-fidelity deployment check evaluated an earlier design rather than the final 32%-improved design.
infographic.paper_title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations

title: Stabilized Isogeometric Topology Optimization on Trimmed Geometries
authors: Haoyu Su, Giuliano Guarino, Xiaodong Wei
abstract: This paper presents a novel stabilized isogeometric topology optimization method for complex design domains represented by trimmed geometries. Minimum compliance is taken as the model problem, where a generalized Cahn-Hilliard model, a time-dependent fourth-order partial differential equation, is solved and its steady-state solutions yield the optimized structures. This approach does not require sensitivity analysis and can naturally accommodate material constraints and complex topological changes. To impose Dirichlet boundary conditions and solve the instability issue caused by trimming, Nitsche's formulation with minimal stabilization is proposed for the high-order problem. Moreover, the immersed boundary-conformal method is extended to handle complex non-design domains, allowing material-void interfaces to be treated in a unified manner. Finally, a three-dimensional biharmonic problem and several two-dimensional topology optimization examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness, stability, and flexibility of the proposed method in dealing with complex design domains.

infographic.key_insight: Stabilized isogeometric topology optimization enables minimum-compliance design on complex trimmed geometries without sensitivity analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports structural optimization with complex boundaries and non-design regions while addressing numerical instability caused by trimming.
method: Evolve a generalized fourth-order Cahn–Hilliard model toward steady-state optimized structures.
Use Nitsche’s formulation with minimal stabilization to impose Dirichlet conditions and control trimming-induced instability.
Extend the immersed boundary-conformal method to handle complex non-design regions and material–void interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: A three-dimensional biharmonic problem and several two-dimensional topology optimization examples demonstrate effectiveness, stability, and geometric flexibility.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish performance for full three-dimensional topology optimization or quantify computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: Stabilized Isogeometric Topology Optimization on Trimmed Geometries

title: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Finite Element Model Updating: Closed-Form Hyperelastic Strain Energies from Heterogeneous Experiments
authors: Kian P. Abdolazizi, Kevin Linka, Christian J. Cyron
abstract: Calibrating a hyperelastic constitutive model for a soft material traditionally poses two problems: an expert must choose its functional form, and several homogeneous tests must determine its parameters. Neural constitutive models solve the first, but either remain black boxes or draw on a library of candidate terms fixed in advance. Full-field measurements, such as those from digital image correlation (DIC), promise to solve the second, replacing those tests by a single heterogeneous one. Two gaps remain: flexibility during training with interpretability afterwards, and a way to train such a model on one heterogeneous test. Here we close both. We embed a constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold network (CKAN) in finite element model updating (FEMU) and train it by minimizing the mismatch between the predicted and the measured kinematic fields and reaction forces. Pruning and symbolic regression then reduce the trained network to a compact closed-form strain energy that satisfies every constitutive requirement. On perforated natural-rubber membranes, the CKANs reproduce the DIC displacement fields with median errors between one and two percent, and transfer to a hole pattern withheld from training. On a perforated silicone plate, a CKAN trained on one stretch profile at a single load reproduces that profile and the measured reaction force to within a few percent. On an aortic specimen inflated under pressure, an anisotropic CKAN predicts the inflated three-dimensional shape. The discovered closed-form energies match the CKANs they replace on the training data and can be compared directly with established models.

infographic.key_insight: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold networks learn hyperelastic behavior from heterogeneous experiments and yield compact, closed-form strain-energy models through pruning and symbolic regression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces reliance on predefined constitutive forms and multiple homogeneous tests while producing interpretable material models for finite element analysis.
method: Embed a constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold network in finite element model updating.
Train against measured kinematic fields and reaction forces.
Prune and symbolically regress the network into a constitutively admissible strain-energy expression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Natural-rubber tests achieved median DIC displacement errors of 1–2% and transfer to a withheld hole pattern; additional demonstrations covered silicone and an inflated aortic specimen.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer beyond the tested geometries and loading regimes remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Finite Element Model Updating: Closed-Form Hyperelastic Strain Energies from Heterogeneous Experiments

title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
authors: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal, Safa Jamali
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

infographic.key_insight: RheOFormer’s failures in Bingham flow prediction can be reduced through logarithmic velocity representations, gradient-aware losses, and a few strategically selected training cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These remedies support more data-efficient neural surrogates for viscoplastic flow simulation, particularly when low-gradient plug regions challenge prediction accuracy.
method: Evaluate RheOFormer on steady Bingham channel flow across dataset structures, numerical ranges, and input representations.
Introduce logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware losses to improve plug-region predictions.
Augment training with selected cases covering missing physical regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved accuracy in challenging regimes, reduced extrapolation errors with few added cases, and accurate steady-state prediction from a single partially developed snapshot, outperforming input copying.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to a simple channel geometry and Bingham model; generalization to complex geometries and other constitutive laws remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows

title: Certified Finite Element Error Bounds for Diffusion Equations with Measure-Valued Principal-Part Delays
authors: Hiroki Ishizaka
abstract: We derive computable a posteriori finite element error bounds for diffusion equations whose highest-order spatial operator carries a non-negative measure-valued delay. Although the delay law is replaced by finitely many atoms in computations, the bounds measure the error with respect to the solution for the original law. An equilibrated Raviart--Thomas flux controls the spatial residual, and a transport estimate on the computed time reconstruction controls the delay-law residual without additional temporal regularity of the exact solution. A cumulative-mass representation preserves cancellation in this residual and allows a jump between the numerical initial state and the prescribed history. The constants are independent of the mesh aspect ratios and of the number of atoms, and inexact flux equilibration and errors in the elementwise residual means are included. We also give a quantile-based budget for the delay residual and a weighted finite-horizon bound beyond the mass-subcritical regime. Under an elliptic equilibration hypothesis, we prove a two-sided estimate for a combined error norm that includes the time derivative. On right-triangular meshes satisfying the maximum-angle condition, however, the lowest-order Raviart--Thomas estimator can exceed the combined graph error by a factor at least proportional to the aspect ratio. Numerical experiments on anisotropic meshes, including a law beyond the mass-subcritical regime, illustrate the behaviour of the residual indicators and the limitations of efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: Computable finite element bounds certify error against the original measure-valued delay law, even when computations replace that law with finitely many atoms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports reliable simulation of diffusion with delayed principal-part response, including computations on highly anisotropic meshes.
method: Use equilibrated Raviart–Thomas fluxes to control spatial residuals.
Bound delay-law residuals through transport estimates and a cancellation-preserving cumulative-mass representation.
Include inexact equilibration and residual-mean errors, with weighted finite-horizon bounds beyond the mass-subcritical regime.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on anisotropic meshes, including a delay law beyond the mass-subcritical regime, illustrate residual-indicator behavior and efficiency limitations.
infographic.watch_item: Although reliability constants are aspect-ratio independent, the lowest-order Raviart–Thomas estimator can overestimate combined graph error by a factor growing at least proportionally to mesh aspect ratio.
infographic.paper_title: Certified Finite Element Error Bounds for Diffusion Equations with Measure-Valued Principal-Part Delays

title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
authors: Keuntae Kim, Beomseok Lee, Hyunwoo Kim, Yong Suk Choi
abstract: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.

infographic.key_insight: Apparent forgetting in continually trained language models depends on the evaluation interface and can reflect head–backbone mismatch rather than complete loss of learned representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For engineering language-model workflows updated across tasks, separating readout failure from representation drift could guide more targeted repairs, though solid-mechanics applications were not evaluated.
method: Compare the sequentially trained head, a fresh probe on frozen backbone features, and classifier-free backbone diagnostics.
Measure interface-dependent backward and forward transfer across incremental-learning settings.
Apply Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT) while keeping the incrementally trained backbone fixed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across encoder and decoder backbones, class-incremental experiments and task-incremental checks showed interface-dependent forgetting; JLT recovered 96–99% of the gap to joint training for replay- and distillation-based methods, versus about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: High recoverability with a newly trained readout does not imply preserved deployed performance or eliminate partial representation drift.
infographic.paper_title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity

title: A High-Order Geometry-Conforming Selective Discontinuous Galerkin Method and Its Error Analysis for Elliptic Interface Problems on Curved Domains
authors: Fang Liu, Yuanhui Liu, Tao Lin, Xu Zhang
abstract: We develop and analyze a high-order geometry-conforming immersed finite element (GC-IFE) method for elliptic interface problems on curved domains. The method uses a triangular mesh that conforms to the outer boundary but need not fit the internal interface. Using Frenet--Serret coordinates, the method combines GC-IFE spaces on interface elements, geometry-conforming finite element spaces on curved boundary elements, and standard Lagrange spaces elsewhere. The global degrees of freedom of the proposed method are asymptotically the same as that of the standard continuous finite element method on the same mesh. The main analytical contributions are approximation estimates and trace inequalities for triangular GC-IFE functions. These estimates are used to establish stability and an optimal $O(h^m)$ error bound in an energy norm for the proposed method, which is based on a symmetric selective discontinuous Galerkin formulation. An optimal $O(h^{m+1})$ error bound in the $L^2$ norm is also obtained under the standard regularity assumption on the dual problem. Numerical experiments confirm theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate a reduction in global degrees of freedom to a fully discontinuous Galerkin method.

infographic.key_insight: A high-order geometry-conforming immersed finite element method achieves optimal error rates on curved domains without requiring the mesh to fit internal interfaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports accurate elliptic interface simulations in heterogeneous materials with asymptotically the same global degrees of freedom as standard continuous FEM.
method: Use an outer-boundary-conforming triangular mesh that need not align with the internal interface.
Combine Frenet–Serret-based immersed elements, curved-boundary elements, and standard Lagrange elements.
Apply a symmetric selective discontinuous Galerkin formulation with proven approximation estimates, trace inequalities, and stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical O(h^m) energy-norm and O(h^{m+1}) L2-norm convergence rates and demonstrate fewer global degrees of freedom than fully discontinuous Galerkin.
infographic.watch_item: Optimal L2 convergence requires standard dual-problem regularity, while implementation must handle interface geometry and curved-boundary elements.
infographic.paper_title: A High-Order Geometry-Conforming Selective Discontinuous Galerkin Method and Its Error Analysis for Elliptic Interface Problems on Curved Domains

title: From Compact Orientation Distributions to Texture Evolution: GSH-Initialized Orientation-Aware Deep Material Networks
authors: Ting-Ju Wei, Chuin-Shan Chen
abstract: The orientation-aware deep material network (ODMN) is a micromechanics-based surrogate for full-field crystal-plasticity simulations of representative volume elements (RVEs). The conventional ODMN learns the crystallographic orientations together with the interaction directions, so that a complex texture may require many material nodes and a high online cost. This study introduces an ODMN initialized by generalized spherical harmonics (GSH), termed the GSH-ODMN. The initial RVE texture is compacted into the \(2^N\) weighted orientations of a network of depth \(N\) by a volume-weighted GSH procedure. They are assigned to the material nodes and kept fixed, so that offline training identifies only the interaction directions. The best GSH truncation order increases with the network depth. The online Newton system is solved with a tree-structured lower-upper (LU) factorization that exploits the binary-tree sparsity of the network, so that the cost per iteration scales as \(O(2^N N^2)\) instead of \(O(8^N)\) for a dense solution. The framework is verified against full-field direct numerical simulations of two Inconel 625 (IN625) RVEs, one with a nearly random texture and one with a rolling texture, under isothermal and thermomechanical load-unload-reload paths. Compared with the conventional ODMN, the GSH-ODMN improves the predictions of the macroscopic stress and the texture evolution. At \(N=8\), the normalized texture-difference index between the predicted and reference textures remains below \(0.03\) in all cases. Finally, the GSH-ODMN is embedded at every integration point of a two-scale L-bracket model under cold and hot bending cycles, at an estimated cost three to four orders of magnitude below that of a concurrent full-field analysis.

infographic.key_insight: GSH-initialized orientation-aware deep material networks compact crystal texture into fixed weighted orientations, improving stress and texture-evolution predictions while reducing online solution cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables texture-sensitive, two-scale component simulations at an estimated cost three to four orders of magnitude below concurrent full-field analysis.
method: Compress the initial RVE texture into 2^N weighted orientations using generalized spherical harmonics.
Fix initial material-node orientations and train only interaction directions.
Exploit binary-tree sparsity with structured LU factorization, reducing Newton-iteration cost from O(8^N) to O(2^N N^2).
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests against full-field simulations of two IN625 RVEs under isothermal and thermomechanical load–unload–reload paths showed improved stress and texture predictions, with normalized texture-difference indices below 0.03 in all cases at N=8.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers two IN625 textures; broader material generalization remains unestablished, and GSH truncation order must be chosen for the network depth.
infographic.paper_title: From Compact Orientation Distributions to Texture Evolution: GSH-Initialized Orientation-Aware Deep Material Networks

title: Generalized Emergence through Coarse-Graining: A Category-Theoretic Framework
authors: Kaiwei Liu, Jiang Zhang
abstract: Quantitative theories of emergence use diverse representations and indicators, making their shared structure difficult to identify. This paper develops a category-theoretic framework for generalized emergence through coarse-graining, without presupposing dynamics, probability, interventions, or specific information measures. System descriptions are represented by categories and coarse-grainings by functors. Generalized emergence requires improvement of a specified description attribute along an admissible, nontrivial functor; an extension evaluates corresponding internal morphisms. The criterion separates structural admissibility from attribute improvement and accommodates several attributes under a chosen comparison order. Different functors embody different observational perspectives, making emergence observer-dependent. Selecting an optimal coarse-graining can partially reduce this dependence, but only under a given attribute and constraints; optimality guarantees neither uniqueness nor emergence. For dynamical models, state and dynamical coarse-graining are defined separately and linked by strict or approximate closure; unification by one functor is a special case. Computational mechanics, causal emergence, and approximate dynamical reversibility illustrate the dynamical case. Two static examples show the criterion at work: symmetry emergence, where coarse-graining polygons improves rotational and dihedral symmetry, and cohesion emergence, where coarse-graining networks raises global efficiency, edge density, and clustering. Each example also contains an equally coarse case that does not qualify: for polygons, one of the two symmetry measures improves while the other worsens, and for networks, all three cohesion attributes decline.

infographic.key_insight: Coarse-graining qualifies as generalized emergence only when an admissible, nontrivial functor improves a specified description attribute under a chosen comparison order.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a conceptual basis for assessing whether reduced engineering models improve selected structural or dynamical attributes rather than merely reduce complexity.
method: Represent system descriptions as categories and coarse-grainings as functors.
Separate structural admissibility from improvement in one or more chosen attributes.
For dynamical models, distinguish state and dynamical coarse-graining and link them through strict or approximate closure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Static polygon and network examples demonstrate symmetry and cohesion improvements, alongside equally coarse counterexamples that fail the emergence criterion.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the chosen attributes, comparison order, and admissible coarse-grainings; optimization guarantees neither uniqueness nor emergence.
infographic.paper_title: Generalized Emergence through Coarse-Graining: A Category-Theoretic Framework

title: Sliced Tensor Operators for Large-Scale Topology Optimization
authors: Pedro Zuidberg Dos Martires, Gustavo Assis da Silva
abstract: Large-scale three-dimensional topology optimization is constrained by both the cost of repeatedly solving the governing finite-element equations and the memory required by these computations. Memory consumption can be controlled through specialized low-level implementations, but developing, optimizing, and extending such code requires substantial effort and hardware-specific expertise. High-level tensor programming frameworks, which support automatic differentiation, offer an attractive alternative: numerical operations can be expressed compactly, while their compilers generate highly optimized code for CPUs and GPUs. However, a direct tensor formulation creates intermediate arrays that can quickly exhaust the available memory. We address this limitation through memory-bounded tensor operators for matrix-free finite-element analysis and Galerkin multigrid. The fine-grid stiffness action is evaluated in overlapping spatial slices, and on coarse grids, the Galerkin operator is retained in a factorized representation consisting of fine-grid stiffness interpolation coefficients and precomputed local operators. This representation permits its action to be evaluated without materializing a spatially varying stiffness operator on every coarse grid, while preserving the exact Galerkin hierarchy. We implement these formulations in topax, a modular JAX library for two- and three-dimensional density-based topology optimization supporting CPUs and GPUs. On a single NVIDIA GH200, topax performs 50 design iterations for a problem with more than 809 million displacement degrees of freedom in approximately $24.5$ minutes. Across the common GPU benchmark, it is up to $13.6$ times faster than the fastest competing implementation and uses less than half the device memory for the largest problem.

infographic.key_insight: Memory-bounded tensor operators enable large-scale topology optimization in JAX without materializing memory-intensive finite-element intermediates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach makes high-level CPU/GPU programming practical for large 3D structural optimization while reducing reliance on specialized low-level implementations.
method: Evaluate matrix-free fine-grid stiffness actions in overlapping spatial slices.
Factorize coarse-grid operators using fine-grid stiffness interpolation coefficients and precomputed local operators, preserving the exact Galerkin hierarchy.
Implement the operators in topax, a modular JAX library for 2D and 3D density-based topology optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On one NVIDIA GH200, topax completes 50 design iterations with over 809 million displacement degrees of freedom in approximately 24.5 minutes; across the common GPU benchmark, it is up to 13.6× faster than the fastest competitor and uses less than half the device memory for the largest problem.
infographic.watch_item: Reported speed and memory gains are benchmark-specific; performance on other hardware and problem settings requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Sliced Tensor Operators for Large-Scale Topology Optimization

title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy: Roles of disordering and nanostructuring in electron and phonon transport
authors: Jacqueline Hidalgo-Jiménez, Payam Edalati, Md Amirul Islam, Makoto Arita, Dmitry Chernyshov, Bidyut Baran Saha
abstract: This work investigates how defect engineering and nanostructuring via severe plastic deformation influence electrical and thermal transport in the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi. High-pressure torsion (HPT) for up to N = 4 turns produces a hierarchical defect structure, including deformation twins at low strains, dislocations and Lomer-Cottrell locks at intermediate strains, and a high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries at large strains. While hardness naturally increases and saturates at ~520 Hv, both electrical and thermal conductivity exhibit an unusual increase upon HPT processing (from 0.953 MS m-1 and 10.3 W m-1 K-1 after homogenization to 1.003 +- 0.005 MS m-1 and 14.4 W m-1 K-1 after N = 4). Analysis based on the Wiedemann-Franz law indicates a modest increase in electron transport (~5%) and a significant increase in phonon transport (~100%) after HPT processing. The phonon mean free path remains small on the order of 0.6-1.1 nm, and comparison with the Cahill-Pohl model shows that heat transport occurs near the minimum thermal conductivity limit, where vibrational modes are strongly scattered. This suggests that the enhancement in thermal transport is not governed by conventional defect scattering, but it is hypothesized that modifications in atomic-scale disorder, such as deformation-induced short-range ordering, are responsible for this unusual behavior. Specific heat capacity increases after HPT, consistent with stored defect energy. The linear thermal expansion exhibits a non-monotonic behavior, decreasing initially due to internal stresses and relaxation effects, and increasing at higher strains due to grain boundary-induced anharmonicity. These findings highlight the complex interplay between defects, atomic-scale disorder, and nanostructure in governing the electrical and thermal properties of severely deformed high-entropy alloys via electron and phonon scattering.

infographic.key_insight: Severe plastic deformation strengthens CrMnFeCoNi while unusually increasing electrical and thermal conductivity, with inferred phonon transport gains exceeding electron transport gains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Defect engineering could help tune strength and heat transport together in high-entropy alloys rather than imposing the usual conductivity penalty.
method: Apply high-pressure torsion for up to four turns to generate hierarchical defects and nanostructure.
Measure hardness, electrical and thermal conductivity, heat capacity, and thermal expansion.
Analyze transport using the Wiedemann–Franz law and Cahill–Pohl minimum-conductivity model.
infographic.evidence_signal: After four turns, electrical conductivity rose from 0.953 to 1.003 ± 0.005 MS/m and thermal conductivity from 10.3 to 14.4 W/(m·K), while hardness saturated near 520 Hv.
infographic.watch_item: Deformation-induced short-range ordering is a proposed explanation, not an established mechanism, and electron–phonon transport separation is model-dependent.
infographic.paper_title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy: Roles of disordering and nanostructuring in electron and phonon transport
